notes: Study 1 and PDF p. 4 identify Experiment 1, but the supplied description does not distinguish individual-word recall, sets recalled, words in correct sets, or longest set; it also mentions reverse-digit span and response inhibition, which are other experiments. All assigned descriptions/locators have this ambiguity. Replication identities and row order do not resolve the original outcome. No single target statistic selected. Printed recall candidates, all main effects of attention control collapsed across test type: individual words F(1, 137) = 7.01, p = .009, d = 0.42; sets F(1, 137) = 9.37, p = .003, d = 0.53; words in correct sets F(1, 137) = 9.01, p = .003, d = 0.51; longest set F(1, 137) = 7.44, p = .007, d = 0.45. Each candidate p is exact (bound e) and paired with its own F and d. Distractor candidates: math errors F(1, 77) = 1.30, p = .26 (e), d = 0.26; sentence-comprehension errors F < 1, d = 0.05, no p printed. Recall outcomes were standardized within test type before ANOVA; printed d retained without conversion. Mood-adjusted recall analyses on p. 245 give only ps < .01 (l) collectively; no substitution for unadjusted tests. Candidate final analytic participant groups from Table 1: operation-span no control 38 + attention control 41 = 79; sentence-span no control 31 + attention control 31 = 62; mutually exclusive test types, each participant performed either test, so combined recall-model candidate N = 38 + 41 + 31 + 31 = 141. The text independently prints final sample 141. Four participants excluded from all analyses for trying to memorize distracting words; only students without prior exposure to the same memory test included. These are candidate sample sizes for field-scope review, not assigned row N. No df-derived N.
